analysis.one_liner: Requires drugmakers to keep selling discounted drugs to safety-net clinics and hospitals through any pharmacy they choose.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, with one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The 340B program makes drug manufacturers sell outpatient drugs at deep discounts to safety-net hospitals, clinics, and health centers that serve low-income and rural patients. In recent years, some manufacturers have refused to ship discounted drugs to outside 'contract pharmacies' those entities use, or have attached conditions on the sales. This bill would write into law that manufacturers must honor the discount no matter where or how the drug is dispensed, bar them from attaching conditions, and let the government fine violators up to $2 million per day. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Safety-net hospitals, community health centers, and their patients gain if the bill passes: the entities could keep using contract pharmacies — often the only practical way to get specialty drugs like cancer treatments to their patients — without manufacturers refusing delivery or demanding claims data. Contract pharmacies also gain a legally protected role. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Amends section 340B so manufacturers must offer discounted prices to covered entities 'regardless of the manner or location in which the drug is dispensed,' covering drugs dispensed through contract pharmacies.

Prohibits manufacturers from conditioning sales — such as limiting delivery, requiring claims data, or refusing to ship to a covered entity's chosen pharmacy — unless the Secretary approves the condition in advance.
Creates new civil monetary penalties of up to $2,000,000 per day for manufacturers that knowingly violate the requirement, continuing each day until the violation ends.

The bill's own findings state that 340B inflation penalties saved Medicare Part D $7 billion between 2013 and 2017, and that contract pharmacy arrangements are often the only means for covered entities to obtain specialty drugs for patients.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the cost: expanded mandated discounts and daily fines. Manufacturers argue they offset such discounts by raising prices for insurers and other buyers, so some cost could ultimately flow to commercially insured patients and premiums — the bill does not address that pass-through. [S2]

drawbacks.text: The bill entrenches the contract pharmacy channel: pharmacies and large health systems buy at the 340B discount and typically bill insurers full price, keeping the spread, so more guaranteed discount volume can increase middleman and hospital revenue without any requirement that savings reach patients at the pharmacy counter.

Manufacturers respond to expanded mandated discounts by raising prices for other purchasers, which can push costs into commercial premiums — a tradeoff the bill text does not address. The bill's findings defend 340B savings but the mandatory contract pharmacy mandate at issue here is the part manufacturers most contest.
The new penalty regime (up to $2 million per day) is left largely to regulations the Secretary would write within 180 days, leaving the practical scope of enforcement undefined in the bill itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who rely on safety-net providers, guaranteed access to discounted drugs through contract pharmacies is real, especially for specialty drugs. But the bill locks in a channel where much of the discount is captured by hospitals and pharmacy chains rather than passed to patients, and it gives manufacturers an incentive to shift costs to everyone else's premiums. It helps a mix of vulnerable patients and well-organized institutional interests, and it does nothing to ensure the savings reach the counter.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 11, 2024 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Peter Welch introduced S. 5021 on September 11, 2024; it was read twice and referred to the HELP Committee.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the status quo, in which they can restrict or condition 340B sales through contract pharmacies and face no daily fines, remains in place. Health systems and pharmacies that profit from the 340B discount spread also keep the current arrangement rather than a clarified legal mandate.

for.name: Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee; wrote the findings framing 340B contract pharmacies as Congress's intent.

for.name: One Democratic Senate cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill, and it never reached the floor.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (industry)
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation of this kind, running a multi-year campaign against mandatory contract pharmacy access in 340B and arguing it raises drug costs for everyone else.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats attached their names — the sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and there was never a vote or recorded Republican position.

industries.note: The bill forces them to keep selling at deep discounts through any pharmacy a covered entity chooses, bans conditions on those sales, and adds fines up to $2 million per day. They argue the cost shifts to other purchasers and premiums.

The bill writes contract pharmacies into the 340B statute as a protected dispensing channel, guaranteeing their role in moving discounted drugs. They profit from the spread between the discounted purchase price and full insurance billing, so gains do not automatically reach patients.

industries.industry: Safety-net hospitals and community health centers
industries.note: Covered entities keep the ability to stretch scarce resources through contract pharmacies, which the bill says is often the only route to specialty drugs for their patients. Large hospital systems also capture part of the discount spread.
